objectives.text: Identify major pharmacologic classes used in the management of endocrine conditions and describe their mechanisms of action.
Describe the indications, contraindications, adverse effects, and clinically significant interactions associated with medications used to treat endocrine conditions.
Compare pharmacologic agents within and across therapeutic classes to distinguish clinically relevant differences in efficacy, safety, and use.
Select appropriate pharmacologic therapy for common endocrine conditions based on clinical presentation and patient-specific factors.
Identify appropriate dosing, administration, and monitoring considerations for medications used in endocrine conditions.
Explain important medication-use and safety information to patients receiving pharmacotherapy for endocrine conditions.
Describe the mechanisms and clinical uses of gonadal hormone agents, including combined hormonal contraception, SERMs, and androgens/antiandrogens.
Classify glucose-lowering drugs by mechanism and site of action, and compare agents on efficacy, hypoglycemia risk, and key adverse effects.
Distinguish hyperparathyroidism from hypoparathyroidism and identify the drug strategy used for each.
Identify key contraindications, adverse effects, and drug interactions throughout.
Apply the full Endocrine pharmacology toolkit to integrated clinical scenarios, and complete a cumulative recall quiz spanning both sessions.

Recap: Session 1 (Nov 10) covered the hypothalamic-pituitary axis, thyroid/antithyroid drugs, and adrenocorticosteroid pharmacology. Session 1 gave us the axis.

Today picks up with gonadal hormones (Section 4) and runs through diabetes, parathyroid disorders, integration, and the cumulative recall quiz.

overview.text: **Suppressing, replacing, or selectively modulating the reproductive axis.** Today the same negative-feedback logic explains contraception.

**Figure 11. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): exogenous estrogen and progestin suppress GnRH pulsatility and the FSH/LH surge, preventing the dominant-follicle development and LH surge required for ovulation.**
This is the same negative-feedback template from Figure 1 (Session 1), now applied to the HPG axis.

prototype.text: Combined oral contraceptives (ethinyl estradiol plus a progestin); progestin-only: norethindrone "minipill," depot medroxyprogesterone, levonorgestrel IUD; SERMs tamoxifen, raloxifene; testosterone; finasteride; spironolactone.

moa.text: **Mechanism: estrogen + progestin suppress GnRH/FSH/LH, preventing ovulation (Figure 11); progestin also thickens cervical mucus and thins the endometrium.**

Chain (Figure 12): ethinyl estradiol plus progestin enter the bloodstream → hypothalamus lowers GnRH pulses; pituitary lowers FSH and LH → no follicle maturation and no LH surge, so no ovulation → result: pregnancy prevented (over 99% with perfect use).
SERMs: tamoxifen or raloxifene bind the estrogen receptor → the receptor shape recruits different co-factors in each tissue.
Breast: blocked (antagonist), so cancer growth is slowed. Bone: activated (agonist), so bone density is kept. Endometrium: tamoxifen activates (cancer risk); raloxifene blocks.

Testes make testosterone → 5-alpha-reductase converts it to DHT in prostate and skin → DHT drives prostate growth and hair loss → finasteride blocks 5-alpha-reductase → lower DHT: smaller prostate, less hair loss.

indications.text: Combined contraception is available as oral pills, transdermal patch, or vaginal ring.
Tamoxifen — antagonist in breast tissue (breast cancer treatment/prevention), agonist in endometrium (raises endometrial cancer risk). Tissue-selective activity is the defining feature of this class.
Raloxifene — antagonist in breast/endometrium, agonist in bone (osteoporosis prevention) — ties back to Unit 2 bone pharmacology; prevents vertebral fracture; not used to treat breast cancer.

Testosterone — replacement for hypogonadism; monitor hematocrit (erythrocytosis risk) and lipids. Finasteride — 5-α-reductase inhibitor; reduces conversion of testosterone to DHT (BPH, androgenetic alopecia).

Spironolactone — antiandrogen effect at high doses; used off-label for hirsutism/acne (same drug as the mineralocorticoid antagonist from Session 1): same molecule, different receptor, different clinical use.

adverse.text: Combined pills: risks include venous thromboembolism, hypertension and stroke. Common effects: nausea, breast tenderness, breakthrough bleeding.
Tamoxifen raises endometrial cancer and VTE risk and causes hot flashes; patients should report vaginal bleeding. Raloxifene does not increase endometrial cancer, but raises VTE risk and hot flashes.
Finasteride lowers PSA by about half, so double the PSA value when screening; sexual side effects occur.

contra.text: **Contraindications: history of VTE/stroke, estrogen-sensitive cancer, uncontrolled hypertension, migraine with aura, and smokers age 35 or older (increased thromboembolic risk).** Liver disease too.
Smoking at age 35+ substantially raises thromboembolic/cardiovascular risk with estrogen — the basis of the contraindication.
"Smoker over 35" and "migraine with aura" are the classic exam triggers for choosing a progestin-only method — smokers 35 or older, migraine with aura and prior VTE rule out estrogen.

Progestin-only options (e.g., the "minipill," depot medroxyprogesterone (bone density warning), levonorgestrel IUD) avoid estrogen-related thromboembolic risk and are preferred when estrogen is contraindicated.
Both SERMs are contraindicated with prior VTE. Finasteride is teratogenic: pregnant women should not handle crushed or broken tablets. Testosterone: avoid in prostate cancer.

interactions.text: Enzyme inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St. John’s wort, some antiepileptics) lower contraceptive efficacy; use backup contraception.
CYP2D6 inhibitors (paroxetine, fluoxetine) blunt tamoxifen activation.

monitoring.text: Testosterone replacement: monitor hematocrit, PSA and lipids.

pearls.text: The contraindication list is the highest-yield content in contraception.

overview.text: **Many mechanisms, one shared goal: glycemic control without excess hypoglycemia.** Today we cover the many ways to lower glucose.
**Figure 15. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): glucose entry raises ATP, closing K-ATP channels and triggering depolarization and calcium-dependent insulin release;**
**sulfonylureas/meglitinides force channel closure directly, while GLP-1 receptor agonists and DPP-4 inhibitors amplify glucose-dependent release via the incretin pathway.**

This is the mechanistic foundation for the insulin secretagogue and incretin-based drug classes that follow — the "glucose-dependent" nature of incretin-based therapy is exactly why these agents carry lower hypoglycemia risk than sulfonylureas.
Diabetes mellitus has four categories: type 1 (beta-cell destruction, absolute insulin deficiency), type 2, other specific types, and gestational diabetes (about 7% of US pregnancies).
Diagnosis: fasting plasma glucose ≥126 mg/dL or HbA1c ≥6.5%, confirmed by repeat testing.

prototype.text: Insulin lispro, aspart (rapid); regular (short); NPH (intermediate); glargine, detemir, degludec (long-acting).

moa.text: **Mechanism: exogenous insulin activates the insulin receptor, promoting cellular glucose uptake and suppressing hepatic gluconeogenesis.**
Chain (Figure 16): insulin binds the insulin receptor on muscle, fat and liver cells → receptor autophosphorylation starts the signal cascade → GLUT4 moves to the cell surface so glucose enters.
Then the liver stores glycogen and stops making glucose → blood glucose falls (hypoglycemia is the main risk).

indications.text: Rapid-acting (lispro, aspart) — mealtime dosing; onset ~15 minutes. Short-acting (regular) — onset ~30 minutes.
Intermediate-acting (NPH) — cloudy suspension; more variable absorption. Long-acting (glargine, detemir, degludec) — basal coverage; relatively peakless profile.
Rapid-acting is given with meals; regular 30 minutes before. NPH peaks at about 4–10 hours; glargine, detemir and degludec are basal. Only regular insulin is given IV.
Sort any named insulin into rapid, short, intermediate or long-acting before discussing regimens — the scaffold for every insulin question.
Glucagon (IM, SC, IV, or 3-mg nasal powder) treats severe hypoglycemia when oral glucose is impossible; place the patient on their side (vomiting).

adverse.text: **Primary adverse effect across all insulins: hypoglycemia — counsel patients on recognition and treatment (rapid-acting carbohydrate).**
Adverse effects: hypoglycemia, weight gain, lipohypertrophy, hypokalemia. Never share pens.
Rotate injection sites to avoid lipohypertrophy; insulin allergy (IgE) is rare.

interactions.text: Beta-blockers can mask hypoglycemia warning symptoms. Glucagon and dextrose: rescue for severe hypoglycemia.

pk.text: Insulin preparations: lispro/aspart onset 5–15 min, 3–4 h duration; regular 30–60 min, 6–8 h; NPH 2–4 h, peak 6–7 h; glargine about 24 h, peakless.
Glargine is acidic (pH 4.0) — never mix it in the same syringe with other insulins.

monitoring.text: Rule of 15 for hypoglycemia: 15 g carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes.

overview.text: Four non-incretin oral cards: metformin, sulfonylureas/meglitinides, TZDs, SGLT2 inhibitors; then the incretin classes (GLP-1 RAs, DPP-4 inhibitors) and the site-of-action map.

**Figure 19. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): glucose-lowering drug classes act at distinct sites — pancreatic β-cell, liver, muscle/fat, kidney, gut, and the incretin axis — each converging on overall blood glucose control.**

prototype.text: Metformin; glipizide, glyburide (sulfonylureas); repaglinide (meglitinide); pioglitazone (TZD); empagliflozin (SGLT2); exenatide, liraglutide, semaglutide (GLP-1 RA); sitagliptin, linagliptin (DPP-4).

moa.text: Metformin decreases hepatic gluconeogenesis: enters hepatocytes through OCT1 → inhibits mitochondrial complex I and activates AMPK → gluconeogenesis falls → insulin sensitivity improves in muscle → fasting glucose falls without hypoglycemia.
Sulfonylureas / meglitinides force K-ATP channel closure — insulin secretagogues (glipizide, glyburide, repaglinide). TZDs (pioglitazone) increase peripheral insulin sensitivity.

Match each drug class to its mechanism/site: metformin — ↓ hepatic gluconeogenesis; sulfonylureas — force K-ATP channel closure (insulin secretagogue); TZDs — ↑ peripheral insulin sensitivity; SGLT2 inhibitors — block renal glucose reabsorption.

GLP-1 receptor agonists — glucose-dependent insulin release, slowed gastric emptying; DPP-4 inhibitors — prevent endogenous GLP-1 breakdown (incretin pathway). Sulfonylureas carry the highest hypoglycemia risk (glucose-independent insulin release).
SGLT2 inhibitors block renal glucose reabsorption: glucose is filtered at the glomerulus → SGLT2 in the proximal tubule normally reabsorbs about 90% → empagliflozin blocks SGLT2.
Glucose and water are lost in the urine (glucosuria) → glucose, weight and blood pressure fall; infection risk rises.

GLP-1 receptor agonists: glucose-dependent insulin release, slow gastric emptying, promote satiety/weight loss. DPP-4 inhibitors prevent breakdown of endogenous GLP-1, prolonging its glucose-dependent effect.
Incretin chain (Figure 20): food in the gut releases GLP-1 → GLP-1 acts on the beta cell: glucose-dependent insulin release, less glucagon → DPP-4 normally breaks GLP-1 down quickly.
Sitagliptin blocks DPP-4; semaglutide and liraglutide mimic GLP-1 → lower glucose, slower gastric emptying and less appetite.

indications.text: Metformin: first-line for type 2 diabetes; no weight gain and low hypoglycemia risk.
SGLT2 inhibitors: cardiorenal benefit — benefits in heart failure and chronic kidney disease, beyond glucose lowering.

**Figure 21. Original illustrative comparison (illustrative relative values, not from Katzung): insulin and sulfonylureas show the greatest HbA1c-lowering efficacy but also carry the highest hypoglycemia risk,**
**while metformin, DPP-4 inhibitors, and SGLT2 inhibitors show a more favorable efficacy-to-hypoglycemia-risk balance.**
Figure 21 is the quantified summary of the drug-class discussion — it answers "why is metformin still first-line": not because it is the most potent, but because of its favorable risk profile.
Semaglutide lowers HbA1c 1.5–1.8%; liraglutide 3 mg and semaglutide 2.4 mg are approved for weight loss without diabetes.
SGLT2 inhibitors lower HbA1c 0.5–1%, cause 2–5 kg weight loss, and reduce heart-failure events (dapagliflozin hazard ratio 0.74).

adverse.text: Sulfonylureas: highest hypoglycemia risk among oral agents. TZDs: fluid retention/heart failure, weight gain.
Metformin: GI upset is common — start low and take with food; vitamin B12 deficiency with long-term use; monitor B12 levels.
SGLT2 inhibitors: genital yeast (mycotic) infections, volume depletion, euglycemic DKA — hold when ill or before surgery; rare Fournier gangrene.
GLP-1 RAs: nausea/GI upset, vomiting, pancreatitis risk and gallstones. DPP-4 inhibitors are generally weight-neutral, well tolerated, with low hypoglycemia risk.
Sulfonylureas: hypoglycemia and weight gain; elderly patients are at particular risk.
Acarbose (an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor, a drug that affects absorption of glucose): treat hypoglycemia with glucose, not sucrose.

contra.text: Metformin: avoid in significant renal impairment — lactic acidosis risk; avoid when eGFR is below 30; hold for contrast dye with reduced kidney function (iodinated contrast).
GLP-1 RAs: contraindicated with personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2 (thyroid C-cell warning).
SGLT2 inhibitors: avoid for glycemic effect when eGFR is low.
Metformin: full dose at eGFR 45–60, cautious at 30–45, contraindicated below 30; avoid in decompensated liver failure; check renal function at least annually.
Thiazolidinediones are contraindicated in NYHA class III and IV heart failure.

interactions.text: Do not combine a GLP-1 RA with a DPP-4 inhibitor. Gemfibrozil raises repaglinide levels (CYP2C8).

pk.text: Sitagliptin: reduce dose in renal impairment (50 mg at eGFR 30–50, 25 mg below 30). Exenatide is not approved below eGFR 30.

pearls.text: Case: a 72-year-old with type 2 diabetes on metformin monotherapy, HbA1c above goal, lives alone, prior fall. **Which class of add-on therapy best balances efficacy and safety for this patient, and why?**

**Given the fall history and the risks of hypoglycemia-induced falls, a DPP-4 inhibitor or SGLT2 inhibitor (low intrinsic hypoglycemia risk) is generally preferable to a sulfonylurea in an older adult living alone —**
**matching drug choice to patient-specific risk, not just HbA1c-lowering potency.**
This vignette applies Figure 21 directly to a geriatric safety scenario: "most potent" and "most appropriate" are not always the same answer.
Drug names reveal the class: **-gliptin** DPP-4 inhibitor (sitagliptin, linagliptin; low hypoglycemia risk); **-glutide** GLP-1 receptor agonist (liraglutide, semaglutide; weight loss, GI upset).

**-gliflozin** SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin; genital infections, euglycemic DKA); **-glitazone** thiazolidinedione (pioglitazone; fluid retention, heart failure); **-glinide** meglitinide (repaglinide; mealtime insulin secretagogue).

**gli- (prefix)** sulfonylurea (glipizide, glyburide; K-ATP closure, hypoglycemia); **-ifene** SERM (tamoxifen, raloxifene; tissue-selective estrogen action); **-steride** 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor (finasteride; lowers DHT); **-gestrel** progestin (levonorgestrel).
**-calcet** calcimimetic (cinacalcet; activates the CaSR, lowers PTH). A stem is a memory aid, not a rule: where no shared stem exists, learn the class name instead.

overview.text: **A brief recap of bone pharmacology, then a new angle: PTH itself.** Unit 2 covered osteoporosis drug therapy in depth: bisphosphonates, denosumab, teriparatide, and raloxifene (a SERM, also discussed again this session).

That therapy targets bone remodeling directly, generally in patients with normal parathyroid function. **This section takes a different angle: what happens — and what drugs are used — when parathyroid hormone secretion itself is the primary problem.**
**If you need a refresher on bisphosphonate dosing or denosumab safety, revisit the Unit 2, Session 2 materials — that content is not repeated here.**
This section is intentionally NOT re-teaching osteoporosis pharmacotherapy — it is new content on parathyroid pathology, so don’t expect bisphosphonate-level detail here.
**Figure 22. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): hyperparathyroidism (excess PTH, high calcium) is treated with cinacalcet to lower PTH,**
**while hypoparathyroidism (deficient PTH, low calcium) is treated with calcitriol and oral calcium, sometimes with recombinant PTH 1-84 in severe cases.**
Figure 22 is the organizing concept for the section — two opposite pathologies, two opposite drug strategies, both targeting the same hormone axis.

prototype.text: Cinacalcet (calcimimetic); calcitriol (active vitamin D) plus calcium; recombinant human PTH 1-84.

moa.text: Cinacalcet — a calcimimetic; activates the calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid cells, reducing PTH secretion.
Chain (Figure 23): parathyroid cells sense calcium through the CaSR → low calcium keeps PTH release high → cinacalcet makes the receptor more sensitive to calcium.
The cell reads calcium as high and lowers PTH → PTH and serum calcium fall.
Calcitriol (active vitamin D) plus oral calcium — mainstay for hypoparathyroidism, since PTH deficiency impairs vitamin D activation; calcitriol bypasses the PTH activation step.

indications.text: Cinacalcet: used for secondary hyperparathyroidism (e.g., in chronic kidney disease on dialysis) and parathyroid carcinoma.
Recombinant human PTH 1-84 — reserved for patients not adequately controlled on calcium/calcitriol alone.

adverse.text: Cinacalcet adverse effects: nausea, hypocalcemia and QT prolongation, so monitor calcium.

interactions.text: Cinacalcet is a CYP2D6 inhibitor. Thiazides raise calcium, loops lower it. Vitamin D (cholecalciferol) replaces or supports calcitriol in deficiency.

monitoring.text: Hyperparathyroidism — cinacalcet (lowers PTH secretion); hypoparathyroidism — calcitriol (bypasses the PTH-dependent vitamin D activation step) plus oral calcium.
Opposite monitoring targets: watch for hypocalcemia with cinacalcet, hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria with calcitriol/PTH replacement — a symmetry worth drawing out.

pearls.text: Case: a patient with chronic kidney disease is found to have an elevated PTH level with low-normal serum calcium. A second, unrelated patient who underwent recent thyroidectomy develops perioral numbness and low serum calcium with a low PTH level.
**How does drug therapy differ between these two patients?**
**The CKD patient has secondary hyperparathyroidism and may benefit from cinacalcet to reduce PTH secretion.**

**The post-thyroidectomy patient has surgical hypoparathyroidism (inadvertent parathyroid gland injury) and needs calcitriol plus calcium replacement — the opposite pharmacologic strategy for the opposite underlying problem.**
Post-thyroidectomy hypoparathyroidism is a classic, testable scenario and a bridge back to thyroid surgery from Session 1 (antithyroid drugs can also precede surgical management).

classes.name: Putting It All Together: Endocrine Toolkit

definitions.text: **Applying the whole Endocrine pharmacology toolkit.** The shared principle is negative feedback suppression by exogenous hormone. For each patient, name a first-line approach AND the single biggest safety concern.

how.text: **1.** The hypothalamic-pituitary-target gland axis is a shared template across thyroid, adrenal, and gonadal pharmacology — exogenous hormone therapy suppresses the levels above it via negative feedback.
**2.** Antithyroid drug selection (methimazole vs. PTU) and glucocorticoid tapering both hinge on understanding exactly where and how each drug intervenes in its pathway.
**3.** Glucose-lowering drugs act at distinct sites (pancreas, liver, muscle/fat, kidney, gut, incretin axis) — drug selection balances efficacy against hypoglycemia and other class-specific risks.

**4.** Hyperparathyroidism and hypoparathyroidism require opposite drug strategies (lowering vs. raising effective PTH activity) — a new angle distinct from, but related to, the osteoporosis pharmacotherapy of Unit 2.
**5.** Endocrine pharmacology is deeply interconnected — spironolactone, dopamine agonists, and SERMs each reappear across more than one organ system in this unit alone.
Connecting back: osteoporosis pharmacology (Unit 2) and drug-metabolism/interaction concepts (Unit 1) both reappear here — pharmacology is cumulative, not siloed by unit.

clinical.text: **Patient A — Graves disease, in thyroid storm:** PTU (blocks synthesis and peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion); check liver toxicity.
**Patient B — chronic prednisone user, abruptly out of refills:** restart the glucocorticoid and taper; the risk is adrenal insufficiency from HPA suppression.
**Patient C — type 2 diabetes, older adult with fall history, needs add-on therapy:** DPP-4 or SGLT2 inhibitor; avoid sulfonylurea hypoglycemia.
**Patient D — post-thyroidectomy, perioral numbness and low calcium:** calcitriol plus calcium; monitor for hypercalcemia.

examples.text: **A cumulative self-test spanning both sessions — use this to review before exams.** The recall quiz is a standalone resource, separate from in-lecture quick checks.
**Recall Q1:** PTU blocks both new thyroid hormone synthesis and peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion, giving it a faster effect on circulating active hormone than methimazole — important in thyroid storm.

**Recall Q2:** a patient on chronic glucocorticoid therapy abruptly stops the medication and develops hypotension and weakness: HPA-axis suppression leaves endogenous cortisol production unable to resume quickly.

Chronic exogenous glucocorticoid exposure suppresses CRH/ACTH via negative feedback (Figure 9), reducing the adrenal cortex’s stimulus; abrupt withdrawal does not give the axis time to recover, precipitating adrenal insufficiency.

**Recall Q3:** smoking at 35 or older contraindicates estrogen-containing contraception (thromboembolic and cardiovascular risk). **Q4:** sulfonylureas force K-ATP closure regardless of glucose; incretins act only when glucose is high.
**Recall Q4 distractor:** DPP-4 inhibitors do affect insulin secretion — they prolong GLP-1’s glucose-dependent effect.

**Recall Q5:** a patient with hypoparathyroidism after thyroid surgery needs treatment — the mainstay is calcitriol plus oral calcium: because PTH is required to activate vitamin D, calcitriol (already-active vitamin D) bypasses that activation step.

**Recall Q6:** SGLT2 inhibitors block renal glucose reabsorption, increasing urinary glucose excretion and creating a favorable environment for genital fungal overgrowth — a mechanism-based adverse effect.

traps.text: Choosing the most potent glucose-lowering drug instead of the safest for an older adult who falls.

Integrated case — diabetes: a DPP-4 or SGLT2 inhibitor is preferable to a sulfonylurea given the fall history — sulfonylureas force glucose-independent insulin release, raising hypoglycemia-driven fall risk.

Integrated case — thyroid storm: beta-blocker + PTU first, then iodine solution only after PTU (never before — iodine first would supply substrate for new hormone synthesis before synthesis is blocked, worsening the crisis).
Corticosteroids also help in thyroid storm by blunting peripheral conversion and covering relative adrenal insufficiency.

Shared concept: effective endocrine drug selection depends on knowing exactly where in a pathway (or which receptor/site) a drug acts — that position determines both its efficacy and its specific risks.

summary.text: **Combined contraception** suppresses GnRH/FSH/LH; no estrogen with prior VTE/stroke, **smoker ≥ 35**, **migraine with aura**, estrogen-sensitive cancer, uncontrolled hypertension → progestin-only. Inducers (rifampin) need backup.
**Tamoxifen** blocks breast but activates endometrium (report bleeding); **raloxifene** activates bone, blocks endometrium; both raise VTE. **Finasteride** lowers DHT and halves PSA.
**Insulin**: rapid (lispro, aspart), short (regular — the only IV insulin), NPH, basal (glargine, detemir, degludec); main risk **hypoglycemia** (rule of 15; beta-blockers mask it).

**Metformin** first-line (avoid eGFR < 30, hold for contrast, B12); **sulfonylureas** highest oral hypoglycemia; **TZDs** fluid/heart failure; **SGLT2** genital infections, euglycemic DKA, cardiorenal benefit.
**GLP-1 RAs** (weight loss; no MTC/MEN2) and **DPP-4 inhibitors** (weight neutral) work glucose-dependently — low hypoglycemia; older adult who falls → DPP-4 or SGLT2.
